description: Somos estudante de Análise e Desenvolvimento de Sistemas e esta é a nossa primeira vez no NASA Space Apps Challenge. Queremos aprender, fazer networking e nos desafiar em algo novo. Temos interesse em tecnologia, programação, criatividade e desenvolvimento de projetos. Buscamos pessoas dispostas a trocar conhecimentos e construir algo juntos, independente do nível de experiência.
summary: FIREWATCHER is a web application that turns more than two decades of NASA FIRMS MODIS and VIIRS hotspot detections into one burning-activity calendar. Raw counts from the two instruments cannot be compared: when VIIRS takes over from MODIS in 2012 the record jumps about ninefold, although the fires did not. We estimate the earlier MODIS record on a VIIRS-equivalent scale, per 0.25° cell and month, and use observed VIIRS counts from February 2012 onward. The validated product covers Northeast Brazil from July 2002 to November 2026, with observations through 14 November. Estimated months are labeled and carry a 90% interval; missing observations and partial months are marked. In a map-first explorer, users pick an area and a period, compare any month with its historical median, see anomalies and the seasonal profile, open the daily detections of a month, and download the detections, the calendar table and the charts. The frozen method passed its pre-set final test: lower cell-month errors than every simple baseline, and level with the best one on regional totals. The landing page also previews a first Brazil-wide run of the same method, labeled experimental and not validated. A hotspot is not a fire count or burned area. This exploratory prototype provides no forecast or risk assessment.
details:
NASA has two satellite records of active fire. MODIS, on Terra and Aqua, has detected hotspots since 2000 with 1 km pixels. VIIRS, on Suomi NPP and NOAA-20, started in 2012 with 375 m pixels and detects many smaller fires that MODIS misses. Both are free in NASA FIRMS, but they do not line up: in Northeast Brazil the hotspot count jumps about ninefold in 2012, when VIIRS takes over from MODIS, with no matching change in fire. A recent month compared with the years before 2012 mixes the change of instrument with the change in fire.

FIREWATCHER is our answer to the challenge "Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots". It puts both records on one VIIRS-equivalent scale and shows the result as a calendar of burning activity from 2002 to today, in a public web application where the user picks the area and the period. The sections below say what the application does, how the method works, how we tested it and what it cannot tell you.

Code, data pipeline and documentation: https://github.com/1kaliel/astro-boys

What it does

FIREWATCHER has two pages, both open without an account.

  • Landing page: the story in one screen. An interactive globe plays hotspot activity month by month, a chart shows the 2012 jump in the raw record beside the harmonized series, and a short "How it works" explains the method. The globe and one chart use a first run over all of Brazil, labeled experimental and not validated; a dashed box marks the validated Northeast pilot.
  • Explorer: a map with a sidebar in three steps (where, when, what). One selected month drives the map, the totals and the timeline.
  • Calendar: one row per year and one square per month, from 2002 to the current month, on a single VIIRS-equivalent scale. Months estimated from MODIS are marked; partial months and months without data are shown as such, never as zero.
  • Area and period: the whole region, a state (approximate boxes), a rectangle drawn on the map, typed coordinates, or the visible map area; any range of years; all detections, day only or night only. A switch shows the harmonized series or the native MODIS or VIIRS counts.
  • Comparisons: the selected month against the median of the same month in other years (the same days for the unfinished month); an anomaly view of how unusual each month was for its place and season; a seasonal profile with the usual range; a chart of the raw MODIS and VIIRS counts beside the harmonized series.
  • Day view: the daily native detections of a month, with the satellite and its overpass times. Daily counts are native and labeled as such; the harmonized series stays monthly.
  • Downloads: the native NASA detections for the selected area and dates as CSV, with sensor, satellite and product version in every row; the calendar as a table with intervals and provenance; the charts as SVG or PNG.
  • Explanations in place: a guided tour and an "Understand the data" panel with what a hotspot is, how to read each indicator, the sources and the limitations.

How it works

  1. Data. MODIS (Aqua and Terra) and VIIRS (Suomi NPP and NOAA-20) detections from NASA FIRMS are normalized, filtered to nominal or high confidence and vegetation type where supplied, and counted per 0.25° cell, local solar month, day or night, and satellite. NRT files lack type: it stays null and nominal/high untyped detections enter provisional counts, which may include non-vegetation sources. Sensor, satellite and product version stay in every row.
  2. Gaps. Likely observation gaps are inferred from detection deficits and compared with available NASA and NOAA notices. This is not a complete observation mask and not every gap has independent confirmation. Incomplete months are flagged; missing data are not treated as zero activity.
  3. Transfer function. In 2012–2019, when Aqua MODIS and Suomi NPP VIIRS observed together at nearly the same local time, we fit for each cell, month of year and time of day (a) a factor that converts Aqua counts to VIIRS-equivalent counts and (b) a background term for the activity VIIRS sees where Aqua sees none. Cells with little data borrow strength from their 1° neighborhood. Terra tells the model whether a cell with no Aqua detection was active, and each month is reconciled with the regional ratio.
  4. One series. Before February 2012 the calendar holds estimates from Aqua; from February 2012 it holds observed VIIRS counts, with NOAA-20 filling Suomi NPP outages after a measured continuity ratio (1.041).
  5. Uncertainty. Every estimate carries a 90% interval taken from the errors the method made on years left out of the fit.

How we know it works

  • The method was frozen, with a written pass rule, before the test years were opened. The final test (2022–2023) was run once.
  • Per cell and month, its mean absolute error is 3.46 detections against 4.22 for the best simple conversion, and 5.33 for raw MODIS counts. On regional monthly totals it is level with the best simple conversion.
  • The 90% intervals contained the observed value in 94% of cell-months of the development years.
  • A clean-clone reproduction at commit 5286248 rebuilt the published calendar and was audited. Early-years and 2026 ingestion were repeated on newer code with matching counts; the complete pipeline was not rerun on the latest code. Reproduction reports: methodology, reproducibility section.

What it does not do

  • A hotspot is a satellite detection, not a fire, a number of fires or a burned area.
  • The series is the early-afternoon and night view of the satellites, not all fire activity of the day.
  • Estimates before 2012 rest on the assumption that the 2012–2019 relation held earlier; there is no VIIRS observation to test that directly.
  • Since 2022 the Aqua orbit has drifted to later overpass times, and the conversion is about 20% high for 2024–2025. This does not enter the product, which uses observed VIIRS from 2012.
  • January–July 2026 use standard processing; August onward uses provisional near-real-time records. November is partial through 14 November. NRT records lack type and may include non-vegetation sources.
  • It is an exploratory prototype: no forecast, no risk level, not for emergency decisions.

Benefits and goals

Land managers, researchers and fire services can compare any month with two decades of history on one scale, with instrument differences addressed and uncertainty shown for estimates. Harmonization does not establish that every change around a sensor transition is artificial. The method is documented and reproducible, so it can be extended to other regions with the same NASA files. Northeast Brazil is the validated pilot; a first Brazil-wide run with the same frozen method is shown on the landing page as an experimental preview (on development years 2020–2021 its cell-month error is 14% below the best simple conversion; it has not had a blind test).

Tools and languages

Python 3.12, DuckDB and partitioned Parquet for the pipeline (managed with uv, tested with pytest); FastAPI for the backend; TypeScript, React and Vite for the frontend, with nivo and MapLibre GL JS; Google Cloud (Cloud Storage, a Compute Engine VM, Cloud Build and Cloud Run). Full list with licenses: https://github.com/1kaliel/astro-boys/blob/main/docs/resources.md

NASA data, acknowledgement and references

All detections come from NASA FIRMS (Fire Information for Resource Management System), part of NASA LANCE: MODIS Collection 6 / 6.1 active fire detections (MCD14ML), Terra and Aqua, 2000–2025; VIIRS 375 m active fire product, Suomi NPP (VNP14IMG), 2012–2026, and NOAA-20 (VJ114IMG), 2018–2026; near-real-time VIIRS files (VNP14IMGTDL_NRT, VJ114IMGTDL_NRT) for August to November 2026. NASA and NOAA mission notices on satellite outages and orbit changes were used to check the gaps found in the data. The published calendar uses the Brazil country files clipped to the Northeast; the experimental preview on the landing page uses the same files for all of Brazil.

We acknowledge the use of data from NASA LANCE FIRMS (https://earthdata.nasa.gov/firms), part of the NASA Earth Science Data and Information System (ESDIS). No data from other space agencies is used. NASA does not endorse this project.

Algorithm references: Giglio et al. (2003), MODIS contextual fire detection; Schroeder et al. (2014), VIIRS 375 m active fire product; Twedt et al. (2023), MODIS orbit drift; Giglio, Schroeder and Hall, MODIS Collection 6 / 6.1 Active Fire Product User's Guide. Basemap: OpenFreeMap, © OpenMapTiles, data from OpenStreetMap contributors (ODbL). Font: Instrument Serif (SIL OFL 1.1). Product DOIs, the LANCE disclaimer and every library with its license: docs/resources.md.

Use of AI tools

AI tools were used to speed up the work, not to decide how to solve the challenge.

  • What AI did: wrote and tested code under the direction of team members (data pipeline, calibration and validation code, the web application including the landing page and the explorer redesign), ran checks and reproductions, reviewed pull requests, structured and edited documentation in English, and drafted texts such as this page from the team's own documents.
  • What the team did: chose the challenge and the approach, proposed the method and its improvements (the transfer function with a background term, the gap mask, Terra as a witness, the reconciliation with regional totals, the blind final test), decided every trade-off recorded in the diary, and reviewed the results.
  • Tools: Claude Code (Anthropic) and Codex (OpenAI) as coding assistants, and chat assistants for structuring and translating notes.
  • Where it is marked: AI-assisted code and documents are listed per task in the repository (docs/resources.md, AI usage), and the diary entries say when a step was done with an AI assistant.
  • No AI-generated data: every number comes from NASA FIRMS detections processed by the pipeline; the charts are drawn from that data; the screenshots are captures of the running site.
  • Plan and research notes: the team's first plan and research notes were written by team members; chat assistants helped structure, consolidate and translate them into English (docs/project-plan.md, docs/spec/). The choices in them are the team's, recorded as DECISION entries in the diary.
